title: Comparatives: as ... as, much, far
titleVi: So sánh hơn: as ... as, much, far
summary: So sánh chính xác về mức độ: much/far/a bit + comparative, as ... as, và cấu trúc so sánh danh từ.
whyItMatters: Task 1 gần như luôn yêu cầu **so sánh**, và Task 2 yêu cầu so sánh mức độ giữa các nhóm: *far more likely*, *slightly higher than*, *twice as many*. Nếu chỉ viết *more expensive* mà không có **much/far/slightly**, câu mô tả mất sắc thái; nếu viết *more easier* thì mất điểm ngay. Đây là điểm ngữ pháp rẻ điểm nhất trong toàn bộ Writing.

sections.heading: -er or more? The form of the comparative
body: Short adjectives (one syllable) take **-er**: *cheap → cheaper*, *large → larger*, *big → bigger* (double the consonant after a short vowel). Two-syllable adjectives ending in **-y** change to **-ier**: *easy → easier*, *early → earlier*.
Longer adjectives take **more**: *more expensive*, *more serious*, *more efficient*. Adverbs ending in **-ly** also take *more*: *more slowly*, *more seriously*.
A few are irregular: *good/well → better*, *bad/badly → worse*, *far → further* (or *farther*). Note that **further** also means *additional*: *further research*, *further delays*.

sections.heading: Saying how much: much, far, a lot, slightly, no
body: A bare comparative is neutral. To state the **size** of the difference, add a modifier before it: *much*, *far*, *a lot*, *considerably*, *significantly* for a large gap; *a bit*, *a little*, *slightly*, *marginally* for a small one.
Use **no** and **any** for absence of difference: *The new system is **no** faster than the old one*, *Is the second chart **any** more reliable?*
These modifiers are what make a Task 1 sentence informative: *Renewable capacity grew **far** more quickly than gas*, not merely *grew more quickly*.

examples.right: Electric vehicles are still far more expensive than comparable petrol models.
examples.wrong: Electric vehicles are still far expensive than comparable petrol models.
examples.note: **far** needs a comparative form after it: *far more expensive*.

examples.right: Rents in the capital are slightly higher than in the northern provinces.
The revised policy is no more effective than the original.
examples.note: **no + comparative** = the two are equal in the relevant respect.

sections.heading: Equality: as ... as, not as ... as, the same as
body: For equal comparison use **as + adjective/adverb + as**: *The exam was as difficult as we expected.* The negative is **not as … as** (or *not so … as* in formal writing): *Renewable energy is not as cheap as coal in this region.*

To compare **quantities**, put the noun between *as* and *as*: *as many students as*, *as much water as*, *as few options as*. With multiples, put the multiplier first: *twice as many*, *three times as much*, *half as expensive*.
**The same as** compares identity or equality of type: *The two regions have the same rate of unemployment.* Do not mix it with *as*: *the same like* is not English.

examples.right: The north has twice as many manufacturing jobs as the south.
examples.wrong: The north has twice more manufacturing jobs as the south.
examples.note: Multiples use **as … as**, not a comparative.

examples.right: Access to childcare is not as widespread as access to primary schools.
The two cities face the same level of congestion.
examples.wrong: The two cities face the same level of congestion like each other.

sections.heading: Comparing nouns: than that of, than those in
body: When you compare a statistic across two groups, keep the comparison **parallel**. If the first noun is *the rate*, the second must be a rate too: *The rate in urban areas is higher than **that** in rural areas* — not *higher than rural areas*, which compares a rate with a place.
Use **that of / those of** for singular and plural: *the income of graduates … than **that of** non-graduates*; *the figures for 2020 … than **those for** 2010*.
After **than** you can repeat the clause (*than I expected*) or use a pronoun (*than me*). In academic writing the full clause is safer: *The decline was steeper than **analysts had predicted**.*

examples.right: The employment rate among graduates is higher than that among school leavers.
examples.wrong: The employment rate among graduates is higher than school leavers.
examples.note: Compare **rate with rate**, not rate with people.

examples.right: Spending on health in 2020 was double that of 2000.
The figure rose faster than the government had forecast.
examples.note: Full clause after **than** — precise and formal.

sections.heading: Comparatives that raise your band
body: **Increasingly / decreasingly** + adjective describes a moving baseline: *University education has become **increasingly** expensive.* This is more sophisticated than *more and more expensive*.

**The + comparative, the + comparative** links two trends: *The longer students remain in education, the higher their lifetime earnings tend to be.* Use it once per essay — it is a signature C1 structure.
**More … than** can also compare actions and clauses: *Cities now spend more on public transport than they do on roads.* Keep the verbs parallel so the comparison stays clean.

examples.right: The more automated a sector becomes, the fewer low-skilled jobs it offers.
examples.wrong: The more a sector becomes automated, the fewer low-skilled jobs it offers more.
examples.note: Fixed frame: **the + comparative, the + comparative** — no extra *more* at the end.

examples.right: Housing has become increasingly unaffordable for younger households.
examples.note: **increasingly** = more and more, in one word.

examples.right: The city spends more on cycling infrastructure than it did a decade ago.

commonMistakes.wrong: This route is more easier than the motorway.
commonMistakes.right: This route is easier than the motorway.
commonMistakes.why: Không dùng **more** với dạng `-er`. Chọn một: *easier* hoặc *more easy* (hiếm), không bao giờ cả hai.

commonMistakes.wrong: The new building is much expensive than the old one.
commonMistakes.right: The new building is much more expensive than the old one.
commonMistakes.why: Sau **much/far/a lot** phải là dạng so sánh. *Much expensive* thiếu `more`.

commonMistakes.wrong: The rate in cities is higher than rural areas.
commonMistakes.right: The rate in cities is higher than that in rural areas.
commonMistakes.why: Không thể so sánh **tỉ lệ** với **vùng**. Dùng **that of / that in** để giữ phép so sánh song song.

commonMistakes.wrong: The exam was not as harder as we expected.
commonMistakes.right: The exam was not as hard as we expected.
commonMistakes.why: Cấu trúc **as + adjective (nguyên dạng) + as**, không dùng comparative ở giữa.

commonMistakes.wrong: The two countries have the same unemployment rate like each other.
commonMistakes.right: The two countries have the same unemployment rate.
commonMistakes.why: **the same** đã hàm ý so sánh; không cần *like each other*. Nếu muốn nêu đối tượng, dùng **the same … as**.

ieltsTips: Trong Task 1, luôn kèm **modifier** khi so sánh: *slightly higher*, *far steeper*, *roughly twice as high*. Câu vừa chính xác vừa thể hiện bạn đọc được độ lớn của chênh lệch.

Dùng **than that of / than those of** khi so sánh số liệu giữa hai nhóm: *The literacy rate in urban areas is higher than **that in** rural districts.* Đây là cấu trúc giám khảo nhận ra ngay là band 7+.
Dùng **increasingly** thay cho *more and more* trong Task 2: *Healthcare has become **increasingly** reliant on private funding.* Gọn hơn, trang trọng hơn, cùng nghĩa.
Thử một câu **the + comparative, the + comparative** ở phần thân bài: *The more densely a city is built, the more efficient its public transport becomes.* Chỉ một câu là đủ để thể hiện range.

exercises.question: This flat is ___ than the one we saw yesterday.
exercises.explanation: **much + more + long adjective** — the comparative needs *more*.

exercises.question: The exam was not ___ we had feared.
The north has ___ manufacturing jobs as the south.
exercises.explanation: Multiples use **as many … as**: *twice as many … as*.

exercises.question: The employment rate for graduates is higher than ___ for school leavers.
Which sentence is correct?
options: Housing has become more and more unaffordable.
Housing has become more unaffordable than before increasingly.
exercises.explanation: **increasingly** is the single-word academic equivalent of *more and more*.

exercises.question: Renewable capacity grew ___ (far / quickly) than gas capacity.
exercises.explanation: *Quickly* is an -ly adverb → **more quickly**, intensified by **far/much**.

exercises.question: The service in rural clinics is ___ (slight / slow) than in urban hospitals.
exercises.explanation: Short adjective → **slower**, with **slightly** for a small gap.

exercises.question: The ___ (long) students stay in education, the higher their lifetime earnings tend to be.
exercises.explanation: Fixed frame: **the longer …, the higher …**. Only the first comparative is blanked here.

exercises.question: Spending on health in 2020 was double ___ of 2000.
The revised system is ___ (no / fast) than the original one.
exercises.explanation: **no + comparative** means the two are equal in speed.
